name: Ap (Apas)
description: Ap (Vedic Sanskrit áp-, plural āpas) is the Vedic Sanskrit word for water and, in Hindu religious tradition, the personified deification of the waters as a group of female deities celebrated in the Rigveda and Atharvaveda.
full_description: Ap (Vedic Sanskrit áp-) is the Vedic and Sanskrit word for water. In its plural form āpas (sometimes reanalysed as singular āpa-), it denotes both water as a substance and the waters as a divine collective. The Apas are addressed as goddesses in several Rigvedic hymns (notably 7.49, 10.9, 10.30, and 10.137) and in the Atharvaveda, where they are credited with purification, fertility, healing, and the removal of sin. As one of the Panchamahabhuta — the five great elements (earth, water, fire, air, space) of classical Hindu philosophy — Ap is a foundational metaphysical category. The Apas are also closely linked to two other Vedic figures: Apām Napāt ('child of the waters'), associated with Agni, and Varuṇa, called Apām Adhipati ('Lord of the Waters'). The word descends from Proto-Indo-European *hxap, surviving in Hindi as āp and Persian as āb.

aliases.name: Apām Napāt
aliases.meaning: 'Offspring of the waters' — closely related Vedic deity

aliases.name: Āp
aliases.meaning: Modern descendant of the Vedic word for water

regions: Sapta-Sindhu (the historical Vedic homeland in the northwest Indian subcontinent)
origin: The cult of the Apas belongs to the Vedic and broader Hindu religious tradition of the Indian subcontinent. Cognate water-deity traditions exist in the closely related Indo-Iranian (Avestan) religion.

etymology.origin: Vedic Sanskrit áp- 'water', from Proto-Indo-European *hxap 'water'. Cognate with Avestan āp-, Old Persian āpiš, and Hittite ḫapa-.
etymology.meaning: 'Water' as substance; in plural and divinised form, 'the waters' as a group of goddesses.
etymology.first_use: Rigveda (composed c. 1500–1200 BCE), in hymns to āpas (the waters).

timeline.event: Composition of the Rigveda begins; hymns to āpas (the waters) included
timeline.significance: First textual attestation of Ap as deified water

timeline.event: Atharvaveda compiled with extensive water-healing hymns
timeline.significance: Develops Apas's role in healing and purification

timeline.event: Brāhmaṇa and early Upaniṣadic literature integrates Ap into the elemental scheme
timeline.significance: Ap becomes one of the five great elements

timeline.event: Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika philosophical schools formalise Panchamahabhūta
timeline.significance: Ap (water) embedded as one of the five elements in classical Hindu metaphysics

related.name: Agni

cultural_notes: Water in Hindu tradition is held to be intrinsically sacred and purifying; this belief descends in continuous ritual practice from the Vedic veneration of the Apas.
